universe_context:
Sir Isaac Newton's law of universal gravitation, first published in the Principia Mathematica (1687), establishes that the gravitational force between two bodies is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the SQUARE of the distance between them: F = G(M₁M₂)/r². This inverse-square relationship is the accepted foundation of classical gravitational physics, later shown by Einstein's general relativity to be the weak-field, low-velocity limit of gravity's true description as the curvature of spacetime.

The inverse-square law correctly predicts planetary orbits (Kepler's laws follow from it), tidal forces, free-fall acceleration, satellite trajectories, and gravitational lensing to extraordinary precision — it is one of the most thoroughly verified relationships in physics, confirmed across scales from laboratory torsion-balance experiments (testing it down to sub-millimeter distances) to the orbits of planets and the trajectories of interstellar probes. Physics curricula worldwide teach F = GM₁M₂/r² as Newton's law of gravitation, and it underlies standard problem sets in orbital mechanics, satellite engineering, and introductory astrophysics.
